full_judgment:
Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury J: On an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 filed by the petitioner, this Rule was issued calling upon the opposite-parties to show cause as to why the proceedings of the Special Case No. 22 of 2007 under sections 409/109 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 pending in the 3rd Court of the Special Judge, Dhaka should not be quashed so far as it relates to the petitioner. 

 The accused-petitioner is the wife of one Engineer Afsaruddin Ahmad, an ex-Member of Parliament, Bangladesh. She is a Director of Bastu Shilpi Group of Companies, a conglomerate of 6(six) companies. However, a tender notice was published in the Daily Ittefaq on 23-6-2004 for sale of numerous RAJUK properties. In response to that tender notice, she submitted a bid to purchase the case property being House No CWS (B) 28, Road No. 31, Gulshan. Out of 6(six) bids, the bid of the petitioner was adjudged to be the highest. Accordingly, in due course, the case property was registered and mutated in her name on 28-8-2006. Anyway, on 29-3-2007, an ejahar was lodged with Motijheel Police Station, DMP, Dhaka by one Mr Shafiul Alam, Assistant Director, Anti-Corruption Commission, Dhaka stating, inter alia, that from 2004 to 2006. Mr Mirza Abbas Uddin Ahmed, the then Minister for Housing and Public Works, abusing his official position and in connivance with some civil servants, manipulated the tender for sale of the properties in Gulshan, Banani, Dhanmondi etc, for his own benefit and sold the same at a price less than market price thereby causing a huge financial loss to the public exchequer. Against this backdrop, a case under sections 409/109 of the Penal Code, 1860 read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and Rule 15 of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007 was initiated. The accused-petitioner was not named in the ejahar and that being so, she had no knowledge about the initiation of the case. At that time, she was abroad for medical treatment. However, after the lodgment of the ejahar with the concerned Police Station, the Anti-Corruption Commission investigated the case and having found a prima facie case, the Investigating Officer submitted charge-sheet against 13(thirteen) persons including the petitioner under the relevant provisions by law on 20-9-2007. On hearing about the tendency of the case in the 3rd Court of the Special Judge, Dhaka the petitioner returned to Bangladesh and surrendered before the High Court Division for anticipatory bail in Criminal Miscellaneous No. 13898 of 2008 on 18-8-2008. A Division Bench of the High Court Division granted her ad-interim anticipatory bail for a period of 6(six) months. Be that as it may, she could not obtain the certified copy of the bail-granting order and, as such, she could not furnish bail bond before the 3rd Court of the Special Judge, Dhaka. Subsequently, she filed the present Miscellaneous Case under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and secured pre-arrest bail on 27-8-2008. Pursuant to the order of pre-arrest bail dated 27-8-2008 passed in the instant Miscellaneous Case, she surrendered before the 3rd Court of the Special Judge, Dhaka and furnished the requisite bail bond on 3-9-2008. 

 3. Although the petitioner is not named in the ejahar, but she has been charge-sheeted along with others. It has been stated in the charge-sheet that the alleged criminal liability of the petitioner is that of abetment punishable under sections 409/109 of the Penal Code; but not a single witness in his statement either under section 161 or under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure has implicated her as a alleged abettor of the substantive offence punishable under section 409 of the Penal Code, Nevertheless, the Court below took cognizance of the case and charged her under sections 409/109 of the Penal Code. The continuation of the proceedings of the Special Case against the petitioner is a purported abuse of the process of the Court and, as such, the proceedings are liable to be quashed. 

 4. At the outset, Mr Md Asaduzzaman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that at the time of filing of the instant application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the petitioner was on pre-arrest bail granted by the High Court Division in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 13898 of 2008 on 18-8-2008 and while she was on such pre-arrest bail, she moved the instant application obtained the Rule-issuing order as well as an order of pre-arrest bail thereon and this being the situation, it cannot be said that she was a fugitive from law at the time of moving the instant application before the High Court Division, though he concedes that there was some sort of irregularity in granting pre-arrest bail to her after submission of charge-sheet and framing of charge against her and for this irregularity, she cannot be fastened with any liability. 

 6. Mr Md Asaduzzaman also submits that following the tender notice published in the Daily Ittefaq on 23-6-2004, 6(six) bidders including the petitioner participated in the tender process and the bid of the petitioner being the highest was accepted by the authority concerned and, as such, she was inducted into the possession of the case property and lease-deed in perpetuity was executed in her favour in due course and she has been indisputably in possession of the property in question. 

 7. Mr Md Asaduzzaman next submits that the bid money to the tune of Taka 2,74,79,850 quoted by the petitioner was higher than the minimum price fixed by the valuation Committee vis-a-vis the case property and in this view of the matter, it cannot be said by any stretch of imagination that she influenced the tender process in collaboration with the public servants concerned and the allegation of influence-peddling against her is imaginary and unfounded. 

 8. Mr Md Asaduzzaman also submits that the alleged implication of the petitioner in the case as an abettor according to the charge-sheet is not based upon any factual statement of any witness and from this point of view, it can be said that she has been roped in the case for sheer harassment. 

 9. Mr Md Asaduzzaman further submits that it is in the charge-sheet that the petitioner along with others including her husband abetted the alleged offence punishable under section 409 of the Penal Code; but curiously enough, her husband has not been made an accused in this case and this scenario is indicative of her malaise involvement in the case by the investigating agency. 

 10. Mr Md Asaduzzaman also submits that the petitioner does not stand on the same footing with other alleged abettors like Mr Ahmed Akbar Sobhan, Mr Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury and Mr Kazi Md Anwar Hossain who are respectively accused in Special Case Nos. 14, 15 and 16 of 2007 pending in the 3rd Court of the Special Judge, Dhaka in view of the fact that those 3(three) alleged abettors have been specifically implicated in the statements of some of the witnesses recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, but this panorama has been disregarded both by the investigating agency and the Court below alike. 

 11. Mr Md Asaduzzaman next submits that the facts disclosed in the charge-sheet having no tangible basis at all do not constitute any offence against the petitioner and the non-disclosure of any offence against her is a good ground for quashing the proceedings of the case so far as it relates to her. 

 12. In support of the above submissions, Mr Md Asaduzzaman has drawn our attention to the decisions in the cases of Abdul Quader Chozvdhury vs State, 28 DLR (AD) 38, Nasiruddin Mahmud vs Monitazuddin Ahmed, 36 DLR (AD) 14 and Shokrana vs State, 5 BLC 611. 

 13. Per contra, Mr Korunamoy Chakma, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the State-opposite-party No.1 submits that although the petitioner is not named in the FIR, but admittedly she has been charge-sheeted by the Anti-Corruption Com-mission and the case is virtually a bundle of facts and those facts can only be thrashed out during the trial of the case, but not in an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and from this standpoint, the Rule should be discharged. 

 14. Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the Anti-Corruption-opposite-party No. 2, submits that undeniably the petitioner is not FIR-named; but after investigation, she has been charge-sheeted and her involvement in the case is a matter of evidence and trial and the prosecution case should not be stifled at the initial stage and it should be given an opportunity of adducing evidence to prove the charge of abetment against her at the trial. 

 15. Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan next submits that in the facts and circumstances of the case, it transpires that the tender process was manipulated to give illegal benefit to the beneficiaries including the petitioner in collusion with some public functionaries and this tender manipulation cannot be resolved in an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and in order to resolve the same, she must face the trial of the case particularly when she has already been charged under sections 409/109 of the Penal Code. 

 16. Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan further submits that it is an admitted fact that the petitioner is a beneficiary and if the Rule is made absolute, other beneficiaries will get off scot-free and this will have a demoralizing effect upon the prosecution case. 

 17. Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan next submits that taking the statements made in the charge-sheet against the petitioner together, it leaves no room for doubt that prima facie it is a case of abetment and accordingly she was rightly charge-sheeted and cognizance was taken against her and no exception can be taken thereto as such. 

 18. Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan further submits that the petitioner obtained pre-arrest bail from the High Court Division in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.13898 of 2008 under section 498 as well as in the instant Criminal Miscellaneous Case under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and it is, therefore, clear that she did not approach the High Court Division under section 561A with clean hands. 

 21. In this regard, in the case of Abdul Quader Chowdhury vs State reported in 28 DLR (AD) 38 relied on by Mr Md Asaduzzaman, the Appellate Division has clearly spelt out the categories of cases where the High Court Division should interfere under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In that decision, the Appellate Division has observed as follows: 

 (a) Interference even at an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so preposterous that even on the admitted facts, no case can stand against the accused; 

 (c) Where there is a legal bar against institution or continuance of a criminal case against an accused person; 

 (d) In a case where the allegations in the First Information Report or the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirely, do not constitute the offence alleged and in such cases, no question of weighing and appreciating evidence arises; and 

 (e) The allegations made against the accused person do constitute an offence alleged, but there is either no legal evidence adduced in support of the case or the evidence adduced clearly or manifestly fails to prove the charge. 

 22. The above-mentioned categories of cases as spelt out by our Appellate Division in 28 DLR (AD) 38 case have been subsequently followed in the case of Ali Akkas vs Enayet Hossain reported in 17 BLD (AD) 44. 

 23. In the case of Sher Ali vs State reported in 46 DLR (AD) 67, the Appellate Division has held that the inherent power may be invoked independent of power conferred by any other provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure and this power may be exercised to quash a proceeding or even a conviction on conclusion of a trial if the Court concerned had no jurisdiction to hold the said trial or the facts alleged against the accused do not constitute any criminal offence, or the conviction has been based on 'no evidence' or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. 

 24. Coming back to the present case, it is admitted that the petitioner is not FIR named. It is further admitted that not a single witness in his statement recorded under section 161 or section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure has implicated her as an abettor of the alleged substantive offence punishable under section 409 of the Penal Code. But none the less, the petitioner has been charge-sheeted as an abettor. In this context, the most vital statement made in the charge-sheet about the petitioner runs as follows: 

 25. So the allegation leveled against both the petitioner and her husband Engineer Afsaruddin Ahmad is that of influence-peddling in getting the case property allotted in her name in a collusive manner. But inexplicably the husband of the petitioner Engineer Afsaruddin Ahmed has not been made an accused as an abettor in this case. A mere vague and nebulous statement in the charge-sheet about the alleged abetment of the petitioner without any supporting incriminating materials on record cannot be sustained at all. It seems that the implication of the petitioner in this case as an abettor as found by the Anti-Corruption Commission during the investigation of the case is predicated upon conjectures, surmises and speculations. Her involvement in the case as an abettor, as we see it, entails a journey into the minds of the Investigating Officers concerned, an exercise fraught with uncalled-for and unwarranted consequence. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, it transpires that the implication of the petitioner in the case as an abettor has been made in a vacuum. 

 27. Undeniably on 12-12-2004, the case property was allotted in the name of the petitioner and on 31-8-2005, she made a payment of Taka 2,74,79,850 and a further sum of Taka 8,24,396 amounting to 3% Advance Income Tax (AIT) in accordance with the terms of the allotment letter of the RAJUK. It is further admitted that in due course, the RAJUK delivered physical possession of the case property and executed a lease deed in perpetuity in her favour and she has been in possession thereof since 4-10-2005. It is true that some of the beneficiaries, namely, Mr Ahmed Akbar Sobhan, Mr Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury and Mr Kazi Md Anwar Hossain etc have been specifically implicated in the case on the basis of the statements of some witnesses recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. As already observed, not a single witness has implicated the petitioner in the commission of the alleged offence as an abettor under sections 409/109 of the Penal Code as is apparent from the record. This being the state of affairs, it cannot be said that the petitioner stands on the same footing with Mr Ahmed Akbar Sobhan, Mr Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury and Mr Kazi Md Anwar Hossain and so on and so forth. So we are not at one with the contention of Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan on this point. 

 28. Regard being has to the facts and circumstances of the case, we find no basis of the argument of Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan that if the Rule is made absolute, the other beneficiaries will get off scot-free and this will have a demoralizing effect upon the prosecution case. So this argument stands jettisoned. 

 29. According to Mr Korunamoy Chakma, the case is a bundle of facts and the criminal liability, if any, of the petitioner can only be thrashed out during the trail of the case and by that reason, the prosecution should not be stifled at the threshold. It goes without saying that every case is a bundle of facts and, as such, those facts will be thrashed out during the trial of the case. We do agree with Mr Korunamoy Chakma to that effect, but the fact remains that no specific incriminating, material has transpired against the petitioner during the investigation of the case. We have already held that a vague and nebulous statement in the charge-sheet about the alleged abetment of the petitioner without a single incriminating material on record will not do. Had any of the witnesses in his statement specifically implicated the petitioner in the commission of the alleged offence as an abettor, we would have definitely concurred with Mr Korunamoy Chakma. What we are driving at boils down to this: the petitioner cannot be saddled with the alleged liability as an abettor without any incriminating material on record. As she has not been found to be involved in abetting the alleged offence punishable under section 409 of the Penal Code in view of the statements made by the witnesses concerned under section 161 or section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, we do not find any earthly reason to hold that she must face the trial of the case. 

 30. In this connection, the decision in the case of Shokrana vs State reported in 5 BLC 611 adverted to by Mr Md Asaduzzaman may be gone into. In that decision, it has been held in paragraph 13: 

 "13  In a criminal case, firstly, any allegation whether in the First Information Report or in the Charge-sheet, must constitute an offence within the meaning of the relevant law, secondly, the allegation must be based on the materials on record and not on mere surmises or suppositions. The process of law must not be used as the engine of harassment. It is found to be so abused, it will be imperative on the part of the High Court Division to interfere and quash such proceedings in exercise of its inherent jurisdiction." 

 31. We have already held that there are no incriminating materials on record about the alleged abetment of the petitioner and from the stand point, we can hold that the process of the Court must not be used as an engine of harassment in so far as the petitioner is concerned. Consequently, the High Court Division in its inherent jurisdiction under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is competent to quash the proceedings of the case, so far as it relates to her. 

 32. In the case of Nasiruddin Mahmud vs Momtazuddin Ahmed reported in 36 DLR (AD) 14, it has been stated in paragraphs 28 and 29: 

 "28. This Court has considered the scope of section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure in two cases reported in 26 DLR (SC) 17 and 28 DLR (AD) 38. The view taken in 26 DLR (SC) 17 case is that the statutory power of the police to investigate cognizable offences cannot be interfered with under section 561A and that section is not to be utilized to intercept or obstruct the ordinary course of procedure as laid down in the Code. 

 29. Proceeding before a Court starts when the Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence on police report or on complaint. Before such cognizance, there is no proceeding that may be quashed under section 561A, CrPC. Process is issued only after taking of cognizance. In 28 DLR (AD) 28 case, this Court considered as to when and under what circumstances jurisdiction under section 561A should be exercised and was held that interference could be made even at the initial stage, when a mere perusal of the complaint would indicate that no criminal case stands against the accused. In that case, there was, however, no discussion as to when a proceeding starts before a Court." 

 33. Reverting to the instant case, admittedly cognizance was taken under sections 409/109 of the Penal Code against the petitioner on the basis of the charge-sheet. It is further undisputed that charge was framed against her under those sections on 17-2-2008. So following the 'ratio' enunciated in 26 DLR (SC) 17 case (Solicitor, Government of Bangladesh vs AT Mridha), we hold that the proceedings of the Special Case No.22 of 2007 started when cognizance was taken against the accused including the petitioner. 

 34. Before parting with the case, we would like to observe that the petitioner did not furnish the requisite bail bond in the Court below pursuant to the pre-arrest bail dated 18-8-2008 obtained in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 13898 of 2008, though she furnished the same therein on 3-9-2008 pursuant to the order of pre-arrest bail dated 27-8-2008 passed in the present case under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It may be recalled that after submission of police report in a case, there is no scope for granting anticipatory or pre-arrest bail as has been held in the case of the State vs Abdul Wahab Shah Chowdhury reported in 51 DLR (AD) 242. This principle was not taken into consideration while granting pre-arrest bail to the petitioner in the previous Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.13898 of 2008 under section 498 and the present Miscellaneous Case under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure probably through inadvertence. In the facts and circumstances of the case, the petitioner should have surrendered before the lower Court for regular bail without surrendering before the High Court Division for pre-arrest bail. However, that is a "fait accompli". In any event, it cannot be said that at the time of moving the instant application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure on 27-8-2008, the petitioner was a fugitive from law; albeit she was granted pre-arrest bail illegally by the High Court Division. We cannot pass the back on to the shoulder of the petitioner alone in this regard. 

 35. From the foregoing discussions and in circumstances of the case, we are of the view that the continuation of the proceedings of the case in the Court below against the petitioner is an abuse of the process of the Court ad to secure the ends of justice, the same should be quashed. In the result, the Rule succeeds. 

 Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute. The proceedings of the Special Case No.22 of 2007 arising out of Motijheel Police Station Case No. 140 dated 29-3-2007 under sections 409/109 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, now pending before the 3rd Court of the Special Judge, Dhaka are quashed so far as it relates to the petitioner.
